title: Note Repeat & the Arpeggiator
blurb: Use the controller's own timing tools to hear a roll before you can play it — then switch them off and match what you heard.

steps.title: Set the tempo first
body: Note Repeat and the arpeggiator both run off the controller's internal clock, so the tempo has to be right before either is useful.
Tap TAP TEMPO four times in time with the speed you want, or set the value in the display.
Start PadLab's practice metronome below at the same tempo and check the two agree over eight bars — not just over one.
steps.checkpoint: The controller's clock and the click stay locked together for eight bars without drifting apart.
steps.tip: Tapping tempo by ear is close but never exact. If you are practising against a fixed BPM, type the number in rather than tapping it.

steps.title: Note Repeat, one division at a time
body: Hold NOTE REPEAT and press a pad: the pad retriggers at the current time division for as long as you hold it.
Change the division to hear eighths, sixteenths, and triplets. Every roll you will ever play is one of these rates.
Hold pad 5 (hats in most lessons) at eighths, then at sixteenths. Listen to the difference rather than counting it — the point is to get the sound in your ear.
This is the same build that Roll Builder in Technique Workouts asks you to play by hand.
steps.checkpoint: You can switch between eighths and sixteenths on the same pad and hear exactly where the extra notes land.
steps.tip: Triplet divisions are worth ten minutes on their own. Most players can hear a triplet long before they can place one, and hearing it first is what closes the gap.

steps.title: Play against it, then without it
body: Hold Note Repeat on the hat pad at sixteenths and play a kick and snare underneath with your other hand.
The repeat is a perfect grid — anything of yours that is out of time will stick out immediately.
Now release Note Repeat and play the same hats yourself, keeping the kick and snare going.
Alternate: four bars with the repeat, four bars without. That contrast is the whole exercise.
steps.checkpoint: The bars you play by hand sound the same as the bars the controller played for you.
steps.tip: Do not chase perfection here. Getting your unaided bars to sound close is the goal; a hand-played hat that is exactly machine-even usually sounds worse anyway.

steps.title: The arpeggiator on the keybed
body: Press ARP and hold a chord on the keys: the notes play back one at a time in the current mode — up, down, alternating, or in the order you pressed them.
Gate controls how long each note rings; swing pushes every second note late, which is exactly the feel the swung lessons in Hip-Hop Lab ask your hands to produce.
Latch keeps the pattern running after you let go, so you can leave a bassline playing and practise drums over it.
Set swing to something obvious and listen to what it does to a straight sixteenth run.
steps.checkpoint: A held chord plays back as a moving pattern, and it keeps going with latch on after you release the keys.
steps.tip: Swing on the arpeggiator and swing in a drum chart are the same idea. If you can hear the arp's swing, you can hear whether your own boom bap is swinging or just late.

steps.title: Build a practice loop
body: Latch an arpeggiated bassline at your practice tempo, and let it run.
Play a lesson pattern over it — Swung Boom Bap or Lo-Fi Head Nod work well at these tempos.
Playing against something musical rather than a click is the fastest way to find out whether your groove actually sits.
Turn everything off and play the pattern one more time, unaccompanied. That last pass is the one that tells you what you have learned.
steps.checkpoint: You can hold a groove over a latched arpeggio for a full eight bars without drifting.
steps.tip: Record the last unaccompanied pass on your phone. You will hear things playing back that you cannot hear while playing.
